questions.q: List Eysenck's three personality dimensions with their high and low pole labels exactly as given in NCERT.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Extraversion vs. Introversion, (2) Neuroticism vs. Emotional Stability, (3) Psychoticism vs. Sociability. A wrong answer that lists "Openness" or "Conscientiousness" reveals confusion between Eysenck's PEN model and the Big Five. A wrong answer that swaps poles (e.g., "Introversion vs. Extraversion") shows lack of attention to NCERT's exact phrasing — board exams require precise terminology.

questions.q: A student writes: "Eysenck's Psychoticism dimension is the same as low Agreeableness in the Big Five." Explain why this statement is partially correct but incomplete, using NCERT descriptors for both.
questions.a: Correct explanation: High Psychoticism (hostile, egocentric, antisocial) overlaps with low Agreeableness (hostile, self-centered), but Psychoticism also includes impulsivity, risk-taking, and creativity which map partly to low Conscientiousness and high Openness. The statement is incomplete because Psychoticism is a broader, biologically-based dimension not fully captured by a single Big Five factor. A wrong answer that says "they are identical" misses the nuance that factor analysis splits Psychoticism into A and C — a common JEE/NEET trap.

questions.q: Rahul scores high on Extraversion and low on Neuroticism in both Eysenck's EPQ and a Big Five inventory. His friend asks: "Since both models measure E and N, your scores should be perfectly correlated." Evaluate this claim using the concept of factor structure and biological vs. lexical origins.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: The claim is false. While both models have Extraversion and Neuroticism factors, Eysenck's dimensions are derived from a biological theory (cortical arousal, limbic reactivity) and forced two/three-factor structure, whereas Big Five factors emerge from lexical factor analysis of trait adjectives without a priori biological assumptions. The factor loading patterns differ — e.g., impulsivity loads on Eysenck's Extraversion but on Big Five's low Conscientiousness. A wrong answer that says "they measure the same thing" ignores the different theoretical origins and factor rotation methods — a critical distinction for competitive exams.

questions.q: Analyse the following case using BOTH models: "Anjali is highly imaginative, enjoys abstract art, questions authority, keeps a messy room, misses appointments, but is warm and cooperative with peers." Map each behaviour to the relevant dimension/factor in both models. Identify which model captures her profile more comprehensively and why.
questions.a: Correct analysis: Eysenck: High Psychoticism (imaginative, questions authority, impulsive/messy), low Neuroticism (implied calm), Extraversion ambiguous. Big Five: High Openness (imaginative, art), low Conscientiousness (messy, misses appointments), high Agreeableness (warm, cooperative), Extraversion/Neuroticism not specified. Big Five captures the profile more comprehensively because it has separate factors for Openness and Conscientiousness, whereas Eysenck's Psychoticism conflates creativity, impulsivity, and hostility. A wrong answer that forces everything into PEN misses the independence of Openness and Conscientiousness — a key advantage of the Big Five.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Because Eysenck's dimensions are biologically based, they are more scientific and therefore superior to the atheoretical Big Five." Use criteria: explanatory power, cross-cultural replicability, predictive validity for life outcomes.
questions.a: Correct critique: The statement is flawed. Biological basis ≠ superior science. Big Five's lexical approach yields remarkable cross-cultural replicability (50+ cultures) and predicts health, longevity, job performance, and relationship satisfaction better than PEN. Eysenck's theory has explanatory depth for specific mechanisms (e.g., arousal → extraversion) but fails to capture Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Openness as independent dimensions. A wrong answer that agrees confuses "biological reductionism" with "scientific validity" — competitive exams test understanding that multiple levels of analysis (biological, lexical, social-cognitive) are complementary.

questions.q: Create a novel 4-item mini-inventory (two items per dimension) to distinguish between a person high on Eysenck's Psychoticism vs. a person low on Big Five Agreeableness but high on Conscientiousness. Explain the theoretical rationale for each item.
questions.a:
Good answer example: 
Item 1 (P-high): "I often act on impulse without thinking of consequences." (Psychoticism: impulsivity)
Item 2 (P-high): "I enjoy taking risks that others consider dangerous." (Psychoticism: risk-taking)
Item 3 (A-low, C-high): "I criticize others' ideas bluntly but always meet my deadlines." (Low Agreeableness: bluntness; High Conscientiousness: deadline adherence)
Item 4 (A-low, C-high): "I prefer to work alone to avoid compromise, and I plan every detail." (Low Agreeableness: avoids cooperation; High Conscientiousness: detailed planning)
Rationale: Psychoticism merges impulsivity and hostility; the target profile separates hostility (low A) from impulse control (high C). A poor answer uses items that don't dissociate the constructs (e.g., only hostility items) — revealing failure to grasp factor-level distinctions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Eysenck's theory proposes three ______-based personality dimensions: Extraversion-Introversion (social engagement vs. withdrawal), Neuroticism-Emotional Stability (emotional reactivity vs. calmness), and Psychoticism-Sociability (impulsivity/hostility vs. social conformity).
Fill in the blank: Imagine two Class 12 students, Rohan and Priya, preparing for the same ______ exam.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) name and define all three Eysenck dimensions and all five Big Five factors with their high/low pole descriptors, (2) explain the biological basis Eysenck proposed for each dimension (e.g., cortical arousal for extraversion, limbic reactivity for neuroticism), (3) compare and contrast Eysenck's PEN model with the Big.
